title: Turning Points: Apartheid from 1948
summary: Why the National Party won the 1948 election, what apartheid meant, the main apartheid laws, and how they affected people's daily lives.

notes.text: Long before 1948, laws in South Africa separated people by race (**segregation**), for example the **1913 Natives Land Act**, which allowed black South Africans to own land in only about 7% (later 13%) of the country. In **1948** the **National Party** (NP), led by **D. F. Malan**, won the whole-white election and introduced **apartheid** ('apartness'), a much stricter and more complete system of racial separation and white minority rule.
Why did the National Party win in 1948?

items: Many white voters feared the growth of the black urban population during and after World War II.
The NP promised to protect white workers' jobs and Afrikaner interests.
Afrikaner nationalism had grown strongly in the 1930s and 1940s.
Only white voters (and a few coloured voters in the Cape) could vote; the NP won more seats even though the United Party won more votes.

rows: Banned marriages between white people and people of other races
Made relationships across the colour line a crime
Classified every person by race: White, Coloured, Indian or 'Native' (Black). Race determined where you could live, work and go to school
Divided towns and cities into separate areas for each race; people of colour were forcibly removed, e.g. from **Sophiatown** (1955) and later **District Six**
Banned the Communist Party and allowed the government to ban anyone who opposed it
Set up tribal authorities in the reserves, later the 'homelands'
Separate (and unequal) beaches, buses, toilets, parks and post offices
Separate, inferior education for black learners, designed to prepare them for unskilled labour
In fact replaced passes with a single **reference book (dompas)** that all black men, and later women, had to carry

notes.label: Key idea
notes.text: Apartheid was based on the idea of **'separate development'**. In practice, it gave white South Africans political power and the best land, jobs, schools and services, while black, coloured and Indian South Africans were denied rights and opportunities.

notes.title: Source G: Dr H. F. Verwoerd, Minister of Native Affairs, 1953 (adapted)
notes.text: There is no place for the Bantu in the European community above the level of certain forms of labour. What is the use of teaching a Bantu child mathematics when it cannot use it in practice?

notes.title: Matching laws to purposes
notes.problem: Match: Population Registration Act; Group Areas Act; Bantu Education Act. Purposes: separate residential areas; classify everyone by race; give black learners inferior schooling.
steps: Population Registration Act (1950): classified every person by race.
Group Areas Act (1950): set separate residential areas.
Bantu Education Act (1953): gave black learners an inferior education.
notes.answer: Each law controlled a different part of life.

items: Families were removed from their homes and moved to townships far from city centres and jobs.
Black workers were arrested in their hundreds of thousands for not carrying a pass.
Schools for black learners had far less funding, overcrowded classes and poorly trained teachers.
People of different races could not legally marry, live together, or use the same facilities.
Black South Africans could not vote for the national parliament.

notes.text: Later, under **grand apartheid**, the government created ten **homelands** (Bantustans) and declared four of them 'independent' (Transkei, Bophuthatswana, Venda and Ciskei), taking away the South African citizenship of millions of people.

notes.title: What forced removals meant
notes.problem: District Six in Cape Town was declared a white area in 1966. Explain the effect on its residents.
steps: Around 60 000 people were forced to move.
They were sent to the Cape Flats, far from work and schools.
Homes were bulldozed and a community was destroyed.
notes.answer: Families lost homes, community and easy access to work.

questions.prompt: Which party won the 1948 election and introduced apartheid?

questions.memo: Any three (1 each): white fears of black urbanisation; promise to protect white jobs; Afrikaner nationalism; only whites could vote; electoral system gave NP more seats

questions.prompt: Read Source G. (a) What does Verwoerd believe the purpose of education for black learners should be? (b) How does this source show that apartheid was racist?
questions.memo:
(a) ✓ To prepare them only for labour / low-level jobs (1)
(b) ✓ He assumes black people should not rise above certain jobs (1) ✓ and denies them equal opportunities based on race (1)

questions.prompt: Name ONE place from which people were forcibly removed and explain why.
questions.memo:
✓ Sophiatown / District Six / Cato Manor (1)
✓ It was declared a white area under the Group Areas Act (1)

questions.prompt: Explain why 'separate development' was not equal development.
questions.memo:
✓ White people received the best land, jobs, schools and services (1)
✓ Other groups received far less and had no political rights (1)
